summary: Four substantive conflict areas exist: cancellation, refund timing, email coverage, and retention. Claude’s preference for requirements is reasonable but only provisionally justified; rewriting the design alone is insufficient because the cancellation code must also change, while the webhook API is complementary rather than contradictory to the email requirement.

claims.statement: The design’s 30-minute cancellation limit contradicts the requirement and API rule permitting cancellation at any time before shipment.
evidence: docs/requirements.md:2 — cancellation is permitted at any time before shipment
docs/design.md:2 — cancellation is permitted only within 30 minutes
docs/api.md:2 — cancellation fails only once the order has shipped

claims.statement: The implementation contradicts the requirement and API by rejecting unshipped orders once 30 minutes have elapsed.
evidence: src/orders.js:1-2 — canCancel returns only whether elapsed time is less than 30 minutes

claims.statement: The implementation can also permit cancellation of an already-shipped order when shipment occurs within 30 minutes because it never checks shipment status.
evidence: src/orders.js:1-2 — the only predicate is elapsed time
docs/requirements.md:2 — the permitted period ends when the order ships

claims.statement: For cancellation behavior, the requirement and API should win over both design and code because they independently agree on the same externally observable shipment-based boundary.
Friday-only refund batching contradicts the three-business-day deadline because a cancellation just after a Friday batch can wait approximately five business days.
evidence: docs/requirements.md:3 — refunds must be issued within 3 business days

claims.statement: The three-business-day refund requirement should win because it defines a customer-facing deadline, while the weekly batch is an implementation choice that must be scheduled or supplemented to meet that deadline.
Sending email only for shipment and delivery contradicts the requirement to email customers for every status change.
evidence: docs/requirements.md:4 — email is required for every status change
docs/design.md:4 — email is limited to shipped and delivered changes

claims.statement: The every-status email requirement should win because the narrower design silently omits required customer notifications without documenting an exception.
The every-status webhook does not contradict or satisfy the every-status email requirement because webhook delivery and customer email are distinct notification channels.
evidence: docs/api.md:4 — an order.status_changed webhook fires on every status change
docs/requirements.md:4 — customers must receive email for every status change

claims.statement: Deleting orders after two years contradicts both the seven-year audit-retention requirement and the API’s promise to return orders as old as seven years.
evidence: docs/requirements.md:5 — order history is retained for 7 years
docs/design.md:5 — orders older than 2 years are deleted
docs/api.md:3 — the endpoint returns orders up to 7 years old

claims.statement: The seven-year requirement and API should win because two-year deletion would create an audit gap and make the documented 2-to-7-year query range unavailable unless an unmentioned archive exists.
Claude’s proposed design rewrite is incomplete because src/orders.js must also replace its time-only predicate with a shipment-aware cancellation check.
Repository history provides no precedence among these sources because all inspected files first appear together in the single initial commit.
evidence: git log output: `9838cf3 (HEAD -> main) init` for docs/requirements.md, docs/design.md, docs/api.md, and src/orders.js

claims.statement: Treating requirements as authoritative is a reasonable inference from their normative R1–R4 wording and API corroboration, but it is not explicitly established by any inspected source.
evidence: git log output: all inspected files share the initial commit

open_questions: Is there an external governance rule, approval record, or versioning policy that explicitly establishes precedence among requirements, design, and API documents?
Does seven-year API access rely on an archive outside src/, despite the design saying orders are deleted after two years?

Is src/orders.js the complete implementation or only a fragment? No code for refunds, notifications, retention, or the documented routes is present under src/, so implementation-level compliance for those areas cannot be determined.
